title: Putting the Service-Profit Chain to Work
author_source: Heskett, J.L., Jones, T.O., Loveman, G.W., Sasser, W.E. Jr. & Schlesinger, L.A. — Harvard Business Review 72(2), 164-174, 1994; managerial article
note: Founding statement of the service-profit chain (SPC): internal service quality -> employee satisfaction/retention/productivity -> external service value -> customer satisfaction -> customer loyalty -> revenue growth and profitability. Puts 'hard values on soft measures' (Southwest, Taco Bell, Banc One). Students learn the causal chain logic that all later tests (Loveman 1998, Kamakura 2002, Hogreve 2017) examine. Framework: SPC (origin). Consensus: ~4,300 citations.
course_use: Core reading for the session on the service-profit chain; HBR, paywalled (WU-Lizenz via EBSCO Business Source prüfen)

title: The Service Profit Chain: How Leading Companies Link Profit and Growth to Loyalty, Satisfaction, and Value
author_source: Heskett, J.L., Sasser, W.E. Jr. & Schlesinger, L.A. — New York: Free Press, 1997; book
note: Book-length elaboration of the SPC with cases (American Express, USAA, MBNA, Ritz-Carlton). Introduces the 'satisfaction mirror' (employee and customer satisfaction reinforce each other) and the customer value equation; reports strongest links as profit-customer loyalty, employee loyalty-customer loyalty, employee satisfaction-customer satisfaction. Supports SPC; useful for case material and for showing practitioner origins (and anecdotal evidence base) of the chain. Consensus: ~830 citations.
course_use: Background/reference book for the SPC session; selected chapters as optional reading; check WU library holdings

title: Employee Satisfaction, Customer Loyalty, and Financial Performance: An Empirical Examination of the Service Profit Chain in Retail Banking
author_source: Loveman, G.W. — Journal of Service Research 1(1), 18-31, 1998; empirical (bank branch panel)
note: First rigorous test of each SPC link using branch-level panel data from a regional bank. Results generally support the chain but with exceptions; calls for testing the chain as a system rather than link-by-link. Good for teaching unit-level (branch) linkage research designs. Supports SPC (partially). Consensus: ~715 citations.
course_use: Core/empirical reading for SPC session; paywalled (SAGE, WU-Lizenz prüfen)

title: Assessing the Service-Profit Chain
author_source: Kamakura, W.A., Mittal, V., de Rosa, F. & Mazzon, J.A. — Marketing Science 21(3), 294-317, 2002; empirical (SEM + DEA, 500+ bank branches, Brazil)
note: Combines a strategic SEM (perceptions -> intentions -> behaviour -> profit) with operational DEA benchmarking of branches. Key teaching point: branches must be efficient both in creating satisfaction and in converting intentions into actual retention behaviour; 'superior satisfaction alone is not an unconditional guarantee of profitability'. Supports SPC but highlights conversion inefficiencies. Consensus: ~530 citations.
course_use: Core reading (methods-oriented) for SPC session; good for discussing how to operationalise the chain; paywalled (INFORMS, WU-Lizenz prüfen)

title: The Service-Profit Chain: A Meta-Analytic Test of a Comprehensive Theoretical Framework
author_source: Hogreve, J., Iseke, A., Derfuss, K. & Eller, T. — Journal of Marketing 81(3), 41-61, 2017; meta-analysis + MASEM
note: First comprehensive meta-analytic test of the SPC: all proposed links are significant and substantial, but effect sizes vary strongly (partly by service type). MASEM shows internal service quality affects performance via mechanisms beyond employee satisfaction; service encounter and relationship characteristics matter. Challenges the implicit rule that firms should always maximise employee satisfaction and service quality. Strongest current evidence base for the SPC. Consensus: ~200 citations.
course_use: Core reading for SPC session (evidence synthesis); paywalled (SAGE/AMA, WU-Lizenz prüfen)

title: The Service-Profit Chain: Reflections, Revisions, and Reimaginations
author_source: Hogreve, J., Iseke, A. & Derfuss, K. — Journal of Service Research, 2022 (online first 2021); conceptual review
note: 25-year review of SPC research; proposes a revised SPC (HRM systems as internal service quality, employee and customer well-being as mediators, different loyalty targets, contingencies, non-linear and feedback effects) and 'reimagines' the chain for digital/AI-driven service where frontline employees may be replaced. Ideal for discussing where the SPC still holds in digital business models. Extends SPC. Consensus: ~67 citations.
course_use: Recommended reading for SPC session / discussion on AI and digital services; paywalled (SAGE, WU-Lizenz prüfen)

title: Perils of Managing the Service Profit Chain: The Role of Time Lags and Feedback Loops
author_source: Evanschitzky, H., von Wangenheim, F. & Wünderlich, N.V. — Journal of Retailing 88(3), 356-366, 2012; longitudinal empirical (multi-outlet retail chain)
note: Shows time lags between operational investments and employee satisfaction and between customer satisfaction and performance, plus a feedback loop (current performance -> future investment, negatively moderated by employee satisfaction). Static SPC thinking can lead managers to myopic, suboptimal investment decisions. Extends/qualifies SPC (dynamics). Consensus: ~63 citations.
course_use: Core reading for SPC session (dynamics, managerial myopia); paywalled (Elsevier, WU-Lizenz prüfen)

title: Social Identity and the Service-Profit Chain
author_source: Homburg, C., Wieseke, J. & Hoyer, W.D. — Journal of Marketing 73(2), 38-54, 2009; empirical (triadic employee-customer-firm data)
note: Adds a social-identity path (employee- and customer-company identification) to the conventional satisfaction path; identification explains loyalty, willingness to pay and financial performance incrementally beyond the classic SPC. Extends SPC with identity theory. Consensus: ~690 citations.

title: Old Signals, New Era: Reconsidering How Customer Satisfaction and Employee Satisfaction Impact Shareholder Wealth
author_source: Zamudio, C. et al. — Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 2025; empirical (stock market, signalling theory)
note: In the social-media/retail-investor era, unanticipated increases in employee satisfaction reduce shareholder wealth when customer satisfaction also rises (negative joint effect), strengthened by social media visibility and industry concentration. A very recent capital-market view that complicates the SPC's 'more of both is better' logic. Challenges/qualifies SPC. Consensus: ~7 citations.

title: Customer Satisfaction, Market Share, and Profitability: Findings from Sweden
author_source: Anderson, E.W., Fornell, C. & Lehmann, D.R. — Journal of Marketing 58(3), 53-66, 1994; empirical (Swedish Customer Satisfaction Barometer, ROI)
note: Foundational satisfaction-profit evidence: quality -> satisfaction -> ROI using a national satisfaction index; quantifies economic returns of satisfaction gains and argues that increasing market share can lower satisfaction (heterogeneous customers harder to satisfy). Supports satisfaction-profit chain; introduces the market share-satisfaction trade-off. Consensus: ~5,880 citations.

title: Strengthening the Satisfaction-Profit Chain
author_source: Anderson, E.W. & Mittal, V. — Journal of Service Research 3(2), 107-120, 2000; conceptual review with commercial examples
note: Defines the satisfaction-profit chain (attribute performance -> satisfaction -> retention -> profit) and argues that its links are asymmetric (negative performance hurts more than positive helps) and nonlinear (diminishing/increasing returns). Abandoning satisfaction programmes is a mistake; modelling nonlinearity adds value. Key framework paper. Consensus: ~1,690 citations.
course_use: Core reading for the satisfaction-profit chain session; paywalled (SAGE, WU-Lizenz prüfen)

title: The American Customer Satisfaction Index: Nature, Purpose, and Findings
author_source: Fornell, C., Johnson, M.D., Anderson, E.W., Cha, J. & Bryant, B.E. — Journal of Marketing 60(4), 7-18, 1996; measurement/model paper
note: Introduces the ACSI model (expectations, perceived quality, perceived value -> satisfaction -> complaints, loyalty), the data source behind most satisfaction-firm value studies. Students learn the measurement backbone of the satisfaction-profit literature. Consensus: ~5,090 citations.

title: Customer Satisfaction and Shareholder Value
author_source: Anderson, E.W., Fornell, C. & Mazvancheryl, S.K. — Journal of Marketing 68(4), 172-185, 2004; empirical (ACSI, Tobin's q)
note: Theorises how satisfaction affects level, timing and risk of future cash flows (Srivastava et al. 1998 logic) and finds a positive ACSI-Tobin's q association with significant variation across industries and firms. Bridges satisfaction-profit chain and marketing-finance interface. Consensus: ~1,400 citations.

title: Customer Satisfaction, Cash Flow, and Shareholder Value
author_source: Gruca, T.S. & Rego, L.L. — Journal of Marketing 69(3), 115-130, 2005; empirical (ACSI, COMPUSTAT, hierarchical Bayes)
note: Satisfaction creates shareholder value by increasing future cash-flow growth and reducing cash-flow variability — the two value drivers posited by market-based assets theory. Supports satisfaction-profit chain and Srivastava et al. (1998). Consensus: ~780 citations.

title: Customer Satisfaction and Stock Prices: High Returns, Low Risk
author_source: Fornell, C., Mithas, S., Morgeson, F.V. III & Krishnan, M.S. — Journal of Marketing 70(1), 3-14, 2006; empirical (ACSI portfolios)
note: ACSI is related to market value of equity, yet ACSI announcements do not move prices; portfolios of high-ACSI firms earn excess returns at low systematic risk ('satisfied customers are high-return/low-risk assets'). Triggered the mispricing debate (Jacobson & Mizik 2009; Fornell et al. 2016; Sorescu & Sorescu 2016). Supports satisfaction-profit chain at capital-market level. Consensus: ~860 citations.

title: The Financial Markets and Customer Satisfaction: Reexamining Possible Financial Market Mispricing of Customer Satisfaction
author_source: Jacobson, R. & Mizik, N. — Marketing Science 28(5), 810-819, 2009; empirical re-analysis
note: Finds statistically significant mispricing of satisfaction only for computer/Internet firms; abnormal returns reported earlier stem from a small group of satisfaction leaders. Classic counterpoint to Fornell et al. (2006). Challenges the 'beat the market with ACSI' claim (not the value relevance of satisfaction per se). Consensus: ~130 citations.

author_source: Tuli, K.R. & Bharadwaj, S.G. — Journal of Marketing 73(6), 184-197, 2009; empirical (ACSI panel)
note: Improvements in customer satisfaction reduce overall and downside systematic and idiosyncratic risk of stock returns — the 'lower volatility/vulnerability of cash flows' channel of market-based assets theory. Supports satisfaction-profit chain via risk. Consensus: ~280 citations.

author_source: Ittner, C.D. & Larcker, D.F. — Journal of Accounting Research 36 (Supplement), 1-35, 1998; empirical (customer-, business-unit- and firm-level)

Satisfaction is better modelled as mediator of marketing strategy effects on performance. Key effect-size reference for the satisfaction-profit chain. Consensus: ~300 citations.

author_source: Mittal, V. & Kamakura, W.A. — Journal of Marketing Research 38(1), 131-142, 2001; empirical (100,040 automotive customers)
note: Customers with different characteristics have different thresholds: same rated satisfaction -> systematically different repurchase rates; in one group satisfaction is uncorrelated with repurchase (r = 0). Satisfaction-intention curve shows decreasing returns, satisfaction-behaviour curve increasing returns. Key paper on nonlinearity and heterogeneity in the satisfaction-loyalty link. Consensus: ~2,520 citations.

author_source: Seiders, K., Voss, G.B., Grewal, D. & Godfrey, A.L. — Journal of Marketing 69(4), 26-43, 2005; empirical (survey + longitudinal purchase data)
note: The satisfaction-repurchase behaviour link depends on convenience, competitive intensity, involvement and income — moderators that do not appear when intentions are used as the dependent variable. title: The Complex Firm Financial Effects of Customer Satisfaction Improvements
author_source: Guenther, M. & Guenther, P. — International Journal of Research in Marketing 38(3), 2021; empirical (~100 US firms, 15 years)

note: Marketing-finance interface: marketing develops market-based assets (customer, channel, partner relationships) that raise shareholder value by accelerating and enhancing cash flows, reducing their volatility and vulnerability, and increasing residual value. title: Measuring Marketing Productivity: Current Knowledge and Future Directions

author_source: Gupta, S., Lehmann, D.R. & Stuart, J.A. — Journal of Marketing Research 41(1), 7-18, 2004; empirical valuation model (five firms, public data)

Central evidence for why churn reduction matters. Consensus: ~210 citations (likely under-counted).

note: Current, non-technical CLV note: why allocating budget by the expected value of customer segments raises marketing ROI, and how data and analytics have changed CLV practice. Pairs with the empirical note UVA-M-1056.
course_use: Pre-reading for students without a quantitative background before CLV calculation sessions.
access: Darden store (price shown at checkout, usually about USD 7-9)

title: Three Empirical Methods for Calculating Customer Lifetime Value
author_source: Zhihao Zhang & Kimberly A. Whitler; Darden School of Business; 2024; technical note UVA-M-1056 (HBP #UV9029)
note: Worked equations and examples for three data situations: individual purchase histories, aggregate data with time-varying profit and retention, and aggregate data with constant retention. Directly usable as templates for an Excel exercise.
course_use: Calculation workshop; students replicate the three methods on a toy dataset.

title: Retail Relay (A)
author_source: Ronald T. Wilcox & Brandow; Darden School of Business; 2010; case UVA-M-0784
note: Online-grocery start-up deciding on expansion into new markets. Students run a CLV analysis using retention and promotion-response data from earlier customer cohorts, so acquisition promotions are judged by the lifetime value of the customers they bring in, not first-order revenue.
course_use: Acquisition vs. retention trade-off; CLV-based promotion budgeting.
access: Darden store about USD 7-9; teaching note for educators

title: The Independent Adviser for Vanguard Investors
author_source: Phillip E. Pfeifer; Darden School of Business; 1994; case UVA-M-0451
note: Classic, short CLV starter case: a newsletter publisher decides whether renting mailing lists to acquire subscribers pays off, given renewal rates and margins. Uses a simple retention-based CLV with discounting. Pfeifer is a leading CLV-pedagogy author (spreadsheet CLV models).
course_use: Warm-up CLV case for students new to the topic (30-45 min).
access: Darden store about USD 7; Emerald Darden collection

title: Customer Management Dynamics and Cohort Analysis
author_source: Elie Ofek, Barak Libai & Eitan Muller; Harvard Business School; 2020; industry/technical note
note: HBS note on cohort-based customer analytics: acquisition, retention curves and revenue per cohort. Muller's teaching page shows an example from a digital game where less than a year after joining only 20% of the affiliate-acquired cohort is still active, against about 40% for email and SEO cohorts. Teaches why channel-specific retention changes CLV and CAC decisions.
course_use: Cohort analysis lecture; students read retention curves and compute channel-level CLV.
access: HBP (price about USD 8.95); search hbsp.harvard.edu for the title

title: Customer Lifetime Social Value (CLSV)
author_source: Elie Ofek, Barak Libai & Eitan Muller; Harvard Business School; 2021; note
note: Extends CLV with the value a customer creates through word of mouth and referrals (social value). Useful for discussing why churn costs more than lost margin alone, because churners also stop recommending, and for loyalty metrics such as NPS.
course_use: Advanced CLV session; the link between loyalty, advocacy and firm value.

title: Customer Lifetime Valuation: Water Filters - A Brief Exercise
author_source: Wolfgang Ulaga & Anna Eckardt; IMD; Dec 2013; exercise IMD-5-0785; 2 pp.
note: German setting (Coral GmbH, home water treatment). A direct-marketing agency proposes a pre-Christmas in-store promotion for a table water filter, and the marketing manager must work out how many new customers are needed to break even, given repeat purchases of replacement cartridges. A quick CLV break-even calculation with a European context.
course_use: 10-20 minute in-class CLV warm-up; works well as an exam-style question.
access: IMD / The Case Centre, about CHF/EUR 5-10; teaching note listed as related material

title: Store24 (A): Managing Employee Retention
author_source: Dennis Campbell & Frances X. Frei; Harvard Business School; 2002; case #602096
note: Convenience-store chain with high manager and crew turnover tests whether employee retention drives store performance. Comes with store-level data, so students can test the employee link of the service-profit chain (tenure leads to customer service, which leads to profit) using regression.
course_use: Data exercise on the employee side of the service-profit chain; follows the Sears article.
access: About USD 11.95 (HBP); dataset/teaching note for educators

title: Who Renews? Who Leaves? Identifying Customer Churn in a Telecom Company Using Big Data Techniques
author_source: Daniel Asamoah, Ramesh Sharda, Pankush Kalgotra & Mark Ott; Journal of Information Systems Education 27(4), 2016, pp. 223-232; teaching case
note: Free, peer-reviewed teaching case. A telecom operator faces rising churn, and students merge customers' multichannel interactions into 'sessions' and use path analysis to find the event sequences that come before churn. Goes beyond demographics and usage data to behavioural paths.
course_use: Churn analytics lab; a good free option if HBP budget is limited.

title: Sears employee-customer-profit chain: estimated effect sizes
author_source: Rucci, Kirn & Quinn, HBR 1998; secondary summary in Lean Management Journal 2015
note: Hard numbers from the chain: +5 units of employee attitude led to +1.3 units of customer impression, which led to +0.5 percentage points of revenue growth. Sears also reported that employee satisfaction rose about 4% and customer satisfaction about 4% in one year, which the model linked to more than USD 200m in additional revenue. Check figures against the original HBR text before quoting them.
course_use: Slide example for the service-profit chain; discuss the causal identification of the coefficients.
access: Free (blog); original via WU library HBR

title: Bain & Company: 'Prescription for Cutting Costs' - 5% more retention leads to over 25% more profit
author_source: Frederick F. Reichheld; Bain & Company brief; 2001
note: Primary source for the most-cited loyalty statistic. The brief itself says that in financial services a 5% increase in customer retention produces more than a 25% increase in profit. The popular '25-95%' range goes back to Reichheld's The Loyalty Effect (1996) and varies by industry. Good for teaching source criticism: students compare the original claim with how it circulates in practitioner blogs.
course_use: Myth-check exercise: trace the 5%/25-95% claim to the source and recompute it with a simple CLV model.

title: ACSI-based stock portfolio: satisfaction and shareholder value
author_source: Fornell, Mithas, Morgeson & Krishnan; Journal of Marketing 70(1), 2006; author PDF (Univ. of Maryland); critique by Jacobson & Mizik, Marketing Science 2009
note: Back-tested portfolio of firms with high and rising ACSI scores (Feb 1997 to May 2003): about 40% cumulative return vs. 13% for the S&P 500, with a beta of about 0.78 ('high returns, low risk'). The Jacobson & Mizik commentary disputes statistical significance, and Aksoy et al. find outperformance only in expansions. This makes it a strong example of the satisfaction-to-firm-value link and of the debate around it.
course_use: End point of the satisfaction-profit chain (customer metrics to stock market); debate format, pro vs. contra.
access: Free (author PDF); JM via WU library

title: Starbucks Rewards: members' share of US spend (Digital IR Dashboard Q4 FY2025)
author_source: Starbucks Corporation; Investor Relations Digital Dashboard, Q4 FY2025 (Oct 2025); FY2025 10-K
note: Quarterly investor KPIs: 34.2m US 90-day active Rewards members (peak 34.6m in Q1 FY25), and members accounting for 57-60% of tender dollars in US company-operated stores. Starbucks says members drove nearly 60% of US company-operated revenue in FY2025, more than USD 13bn. A real company reporting loyalty KPIs to investors.
course_use: Loyalty-programme KPIs in investor communication; students compute member vs. non-member spend and discuss selection effects.

title: Amazon Prime members vs. non-members: annual spend (CIRP survey)
author_source: Consumer Intelligence Research Partners (CIRP), reported by Fortune, Jan 2019
note: Prime members spent about USD 1,400 a year vs. USD 600 for non-members (2018), shopped 26 vs. 14 times a year, and spent USD 55 vs. 42 per visit. The year before the figures were USD 1,300 vs. 700. Based on a survey of 500 Amazon buyers, so it shows both the share-of-wallet effect of paid loyalty and the self-selection problem.
course_use: Discussion: does Prime create loyalty and share of wallet, or attract heavy buyers? Decompose spend into frequency and basket size.
access: Free (may be behind the Fortune paywall)

title: Peloton: churn disclosure and redefinition (FY2025 10-K)
author_source: Peloton Interactive; Form 10-K FY2025 (June 2025) and Q4 FY2025 shareholder letter; SEC EDGAR
note: Peloton reports 'Average Net Monthly Paid Connected Fitness Subscription Churn': 1.4% in Q2, 1.2% in Q3 and 1.8% in Q4 FY25 (1.9% in Q4 FY24). The 10-K gives the exact formula, and since FY2025 a paused subscription counts as churn. Shows how churn metric definitions affect the numbers reported to investors.
course_use: Students recompute implied lifetime (1/churn) and discuss how definition changes affect the reported KPI.

title: Peloton IPO prospectus: lifetime value from churn
author_source: Peloton Interactive; Form S-1/A, 2019; SEC EDGAR
note: The S-1 discloses Peloton's own LTV logic: monthly fee (USD 39) x implied subscription lifetime (1/average net monthly churn, then about 0.65%) x contribution margin, compared with customer acquisition cost. A real-world version of the textbook CLV = margin / churn formula used to persuade IPO investors.
course_use: CLV formula in practice; critique the assumption of constant churn and the missing discounting.

title: Wayfair: customer-based corporate valuation (Theta Equity Partners)
author_source: Daniel McCarthy & Peter Fader, Theta Equity Partners; 'One-Year Retrospective on Wayfair', 2018; see also Wharton Knowledge coverage
note: Values a listed e-commerce firm from public customer disclosures (acquisition, repeat purchase, spend). Wayfair spent about USD 69-80 in advertising per new customer but earned less afterwards, giving an estimated loss of about USD 10 (2017) and later about USD 19 per acquired customer. The fair-value estimate of USD 10.23 compares with a stock price of USD 81.75 to 128.53. Shows that churn and retention drive firm value.
course_use: Capstone example for 'customer metrics to firm value'; students rebuild a simple customer-based valuation.

title: Streaming churn and 'serial churners' (Antenna data)
author_source: Antenna subscription analytics, reported in Sinclair/ABC affiliate news (2024) and Senal News (Jan 2025)
note: US premium SVOD: monthly churn rose from 5.1% (Nov 2022) to 6.3% (Nov 2023). In 2024, 29.5m 'serial churners' (three or more cancellations in two years) made up 23% of subscribers but 41% of gross adds and 42% of cancellations. One in four cancellers resubscribes within four months, and one in two within two years. Useful for discussing churn heterogeneity and win-back.
course_use: Subscription churn benchmarks; segment-specific CLV; resubscription as a challenge to the 'lost for good' assumption.

title: Netflix stops reporting subscriber numbers (from Q1 2025)
author_source: Netflix Inc.; Q4 2024 shareholder letter (Jan 2025); Investor Relations
note: Netflix announced it would no longer report quarterly paid memberships and would focus on revenue and engagement. A current example for discussing which customer metrics (subscribers, churn, ARM) firms disclose to investors, and why customer-based valuation depends on such disclosures.
course_use: Discussion: should firms disclose customer metrics? Link to customer-based corporate valuation and the Netflix Darden case.

title: jö Bonus Club (REWE Group Austria): Austria's largest loyalty coalition
author_source: REWE International / Unser Ö-Bonus Club GmbH; press coverage news.at (2025), Salzburg24 (July 2025), medianet Retail dossier (May 2024)

title: PAYBACK Germany: coalition programme key figures
author_source: PAYBACK GmbH; press releases (payback.group) and Lobbyregister audit statement 2025; mobiflip coverage
note: More than 35m active users in Germany (2025), app used by more than 18m, more than 700 partner firms, EUR 46bn of point-earning sales (2025). In 2024, 58.3bn points (EUR 583m) were collected and about 95% redeemed. The partner switch from REWE/Penny to EDEKA/Netto is a natural experiment in coalition loyalty and share of wallet.
course_use: Compare with jö Bonus Club; discuss what happens to customer loyalty when a grocery anchor partner leaves the coalition.

title: Lufthansa Miles & More: programme scale and partner economics
author_source: Miles & More GmbH; 'Unternehmensstory' EN 2024 (PDF); frankfurtflyer.de on monetisation plans
note: More than 36m members, more than 175 partners including 40 airlines. The programme is run as a separate profit centre (100% Lufthansa subsidiary) that sells miles to partners such as the Deutsche Bank co-branded credit card. Lufthansa's stated goal of turning Miles & More into a cash cow on the US model is a good example of loyalty programmes as businesses in their own right.
course_use: Discussion of loyalty-programme business models; status tiers and switching costs in a DACH context.

title: Tesco Clubcard and dunnhumby: the value of loyalty data
author_source: Harvard Digital Initiative (D3) student analysis 'dunnhumby: how Tesco destroyed GBP 1.3bn of value in 9 months'; Clive Humby interview (CustomerThink)
note: Data-rich history: Tesco bought 53% of dunnhumby for GBP 30m (2001), 84% (2006) and 100% (2010). Data from about 16m Clubcard users helped Tesco overtake Sainsbury's. The sale value fell from GBP 2bn to about GBP 1bn once data exclusivity was capped and the Kroger joint venture ended. Shows how the value of loyalty data depends on exclusivity.
course_use: Loyalty programme as a data asset; discuss the 'Clubcard prices' strategy and the value of customer data.

title: Harrah's Total Rewards: from 36% share of wallet to data-driven loyalty
author_source: iGaming Business interview with Gary Loveman; ICMR case summary 'Harrah's CRM Strategy'; Harrah's annual report 2002
note: In 1997 Harrah's captured only 36% of its customers' annual gaming budget. The tiered Total Rewards programme (points earned on gaming, hotel, dining and shows) aimed to raise cross-property share of wallet, and the company reported 16 straight quarters of same-store revenue growth. A standard illustration of share of wallet as a performance metric.
course_use: Share-of-wallet calculation example; set up for the HBS Harrah's case.

title: Wallet Allocation Rule: satisfaction and NPS vs. share of wallet
author_source: Keiningham, Aksoy, Buoye & Cooil; 'Customer Loyalty Isn't Enough. Grow Your Share of Wallet', HBR Oct 2011, pp. 35-37 (author PDF Vanderbilt); Ipsos summary; book Wiley 2015
note: Firm-level evidence from Ipsos data: satisfaction and NPS changes correlate only about 0.1 with changes in share of wallet, while a rank-based Wallet Allocation Rule score correlates above 0.9 with share of wallet in levels and about 0.8 in changes. Students can compute WAR = (1 - rank/(number of brands + 1)) x 2/number of brands in class.
course_use: Share-of-wallet session; in-class survey with WAR calculation; critique of single-metric loyalty (NPS).

title: RTR Telekom Monitor: number porting and switching in the Austrian mobile market
author_source: RTR (Rundfunk und Telekom Regulierungs-GmbH); RTR Telekom Monitor Jahresbericht 2023 (published July 2024) and open-data tables
note: Official Austrian data on market shares of A1, Magenta and Drei, prices and mobile number porting (Portierungen), which are a lower bound for switching (churn) between operators. Tables are available as open data, so students can work with a real Austrian churn proxy.
course_use: Austrian telecom churn exercise: compute porting rates by operator and relate them to price indices.

title: A1 Group (Telekom Austria): mobile churn in quarterly results
author_source: A1 Group; results presentations Q4 2024 and earlier quarterly reports (e.g., Q4 2021: mobile churn 1.6% in Q4, 1.3% for the full year; Q4 2019: 2.0% / 1.7%)
note: Austrian listed telecom that reports churn, postpaid share (86% in Q4 2024), subscribers (27.1m excluding M2M) and ARPU by country. Lets students build a CLV per subscriber from published KPIs (ARPU x margin / churn) and compare markets.
course_use: Excel exercise: CLV per mobile subscriber across A1 markets; link to RTR data.

title: Sky VIP: tenure-based loyalty programme to reduce churn
author_source: WARC / DMA Awards case 'Sky VIP: your loyalty programme'
note: Pay-TV example: data showed that more than half of lapsed Sky subscribers cited lack of recognition as a reason for leaving. Sky built a tenure-tiered programme ('the longer you're with us, the better it gets'). A good example of a churn-reason analysis turned into a retention programme design.
course_use: Retention programme design discussion; contrast reactive save offers with proactive recognition.
access: WARC subscription (check WU licence); summary free

title: nTelos: telecom customer retention modelling (Elder Research case study)
author_source: Elder Research; vendor case study PDF
note: Short practitioner case of a regional US wireless carrier that used predictive churn models to target retention offers. Shows the full chain from model to campaign to measured savings. A vendor source, so a useful exercise in critical reading of claimed ROI.
course_use: Short reading on churn-model deployment; discuss how to evaluate vendor ROI claims (control groups).

title: Booking.com: 'Winning Some Churners Back' (PyData Amsterdam 2018)
author_source: Ferran Elias, Booking.com; PyData Amsterdam 2018; conference talk (video, about 35 min)
note: Industry talk: Booking.com predicts each customer's probability of churning within a time window and runs incentive offers through an experimentation (A/B) framework based on that churn score. Shows how churn prediction connects to causal testing of retention offers in a European tech firm.
course_use: Video in class or flipped classroom; connects to the Teleko exercise (risk vs. uplift).

title: KKBox churn prediction challenge (WSDM Cup 2018, Kaggle)
author_source: KKBox (Asian music streaming) & WSDM; Kaggle competition, Sept-Dec 2017; dataset mirror on Mendeley Data
note: Real subscription data: predict whether a user renews within 30 days after expiry, with about 1m training users, transactions, member data and about 30m daily listening logs. Public solutions (XGBoost, survival models; arXiv 1802.03396) provide benchmarks. 575 teams took part.
course_use: Project dataset for a churn-modelling assignment in R or Python.

title: Telco Customer Churn (IBM sample dataset on Kaggle)
author_source: IBM Cognos Analytics sample data; Kaggle user 'blastchar'; mirrors on OpenML and Hugging Face
note: 7,043 fictional telecom customers in California, 21 columns (contract type, tenure, services, payment method, monthly charges, churn flag). The standard teaching dataset: students can show that month-to-month contracts and electronic payment are associated with high churn, then compute CLV by segment.
course_use: Introductory churn lab (logistic regression, survival curves by contract type).

title: Praxisbeispiel: Telko-Kundenabgang-Vorhersage (deutschsprachiges Tutorial)
author_source: AI-Tutorial (Read the Docs), German-language tutorial using the IBM Telco churn dataset
note: German-language, step-by-step Python notebook on churn prediction for contract customers. A ready-made German teaching resource for students who prefer German materials; uses the same data as the Kaggle Telco dataset.
course_use: Self-study for German-speaking students before the churn lab.

title: Lifetimes (Python) and BTYD (R): open-source CLV for non-contractual settings
author_source: Cameron Davidson-Pilon, 'lifetimes' library (GitHub/PyPI); BTYD R package; README links Peter Fader's lecture and Roberto Medri's 'CLV at Etsy' presentation
note: Implements BG/NBD, Pareto/NBD and Gamma-Gamma models on the CDNOW dataset (included), so students can estimate probability-alive, expected purchases and CLV in a few lines of code. The Etsy presentation is a documented company application of BG/NBD-based CLV in e-commerce.
course_use: Lab on 'buy-till-you-die' models for non-contractual churn (when is a customer lost?).

title: ASOS: customer lifetime value prediction in production
author_source: Chamberlain, Cardoso, Liu, Pagliari & Deisenroth (ASOS.com); 'Customer Lifetime Value Prediction Using Embeddings', KDD 2017 / arXiv 1703.02596
note: European online fashion retailer (a Zalando competitor) documents its deployed CLV system: daily predictions for every customer with a random forest on 132 handcrafted features, label = net spend (sales minus returns) over 12 months. A neural-network variant was more accurate but too costly to run. A rare, honest industry account of CLV in production, including the cost-benefit decision.
course_use: Reading for the analytics session: how CLV is operationalised (returns, horizon, features) in European e-commerce.

title: Sephora Beauty Insider: tiered loyalty and revenue share
author_source: Industry articles (Alviere; trybeans) on Sephora Beauty Insider, launched 2007
note: Points-plus-tiers programme (Insider / VIB / Rouge) with an estimated more than 31m members, said to account for 'a majority' of Sephora's revenue (not officially disclosed). A good example for discussing tier design and status, with a reminder to students that these numbers are estimates and not company disclosures.
course_use: Tier design and status-based loyalty; source criticism (estimates vs. disclosures).

title: CLVTools (R package) v0.12.1
author_source: Patrick Bachmann, Niels Kuebler, Markus Meierer, Jeffrey Naef, E. Shin Oblander, Patrik Schilter (Swiss academic team, not WU); CRAN, released 2025-11-06
note: Probabilistic customer-base analysis in R: Pareto/NBD, BG/NBD and Gamma/Gompertz/NBD (with time-invariant and time-varying covariates) plus Gamma-Gamma spending model. Students can fit Pareto/NBD on the built-in apparelTrans cohort (250 customers), predict expected transactions and P(alive), add covariates such as marketing contacts, and compute customer-level CLV and customer equity. Fast C++ back end; vignettes include a walkthrough and an 'intuitive explanations' primer (www.clvtools.com).
course_use: Core R tool for the CLV/BTYD session; free, GPL-3; install.packages('CLVTools').

title: BTYDplus (R package) v1.2.0
author_source: Michael Platzer (WU Vienna PhD, with Thomas Reutterer); CRAN, released 2021-01-21; GitHub mplatzer/BTYDplus
note: Extends BTYD with MBG/NBD, (M)BG/CNBD-k, Pareto/NB and the hierarchical Bayesian Pareto/GGG, which uses the regularity of intertransaction timing (Platzer & Reutterer 2016, Marketing Science). Ships the 'groceryElog' and 'donationsSummary' data and a CDNOW elog. Students can compare forecast accuracy of BG/NBD vs Pareto/GGG on a holdout period and plot timing patterns. A good WU link for the course.
course_use: Use for the advanced BTYD lab; CRAN, GPL-3; vignette 'BTYDplus-HowTo' walks through all models.

title: BTYD (R package) v2.4.3
author_source: Dziurzynski, Wadsworth, McCarthy; contributors Fader, Hardie, Feit, Gopalakrishnan; CRAN, released 2021-11-17
note: Classic 'Buy 'Til You Die' implementation: Pareto/NBD, BG/NBD and BG/BB, plus Gamma-Gamma spend. Ships the CDNOW sample. Students can rebuild Fader, Hardie and Lee's CDNOW analysis step by step: calibration/holdout split, tracking plots, conditional expectations, and DERT/CLV. Mature but no longer actively developed; prefer CLVTools for speed.
course_use: Good for replicating textbook BTYD figures; CRAN, GPL-3.

title: PyMC-Marketing (Python) v1.2.0, CLV module
author_source: PyMC Labs; PyPI release 2026-09-29; Apache-2.0
note: Bayesian CLV models in Python: BetaGeoModel (BG/NBD), ParetoNBDModel, ModifiedBetaGeo, BetaGeoBetaBinom (BG/BB), shifted-beta-geometric for contractual churn (ShiftedBetaGeoModel on cohort data), and GammaGammaModel for spend. Students can fit BG/NBD to CDNOW with full posterior uncertainty, compute P(alive) and expected purchases, and discount spend to CLV with credible intervals. Same library covers MMM, so it connects retention to marketing budgets.
course_use: Main Python tool for the CLV lab; pip install pymc-marketing; free.

title: lifetimes (Python) v0.11.3 (archived) and its successor btyd v0.1b3
author_source: Cameron Davidson-Pilon (lifetimes, MIT, last release 2020-07-06); Colt Allen (btyd, Apache-2.0, beta 2022-11-08)
note: lifetimes is the well-known BG/NBD, Pareto/NBD, MBG/NBD and Gamma-Gamma library with RFM summary helpers (summary_data_from_transaction_data) and calibration/holdout plots. Many online tutorials use it. It is no longer maintained, and the btyd fork (github.com/ColtAllen/btyd) is also inactive. Students can still use it to read older notebooks, but new work should use PyMC-Marketing, whose CLV API was designed as the replacement.
course_use: Mention as legacy; check compatibility with current pandas/NumPy before using it in class.

title: lifelines (Python) v0.30.3
author_source: Cameron Davidson-Pilon; PyPI release 2026-03-05; MIT
note: Survival analysis for churn timing: Kaplan-Meier retention curves by segment, Cox proportional hazards, Weibull AFT, and time-varying covariates. Students can treat 'tenure' and 'Churn' in the IBM Telco data as duration and event, plot survival by contract type, and estimate hazard ratios for drivers such as payment method or tech support.
course_use: Python churn-as-survival lab; pip install lifelines.

title: scikit-survival (Python) v0.28.0
author_source: Sebastian Pölsterl; PyPI release 2026-07-05; GPL-3.0-or-later
note: Machine-learning survival models (random survival forests, gradient-boosted Cox, survival SVMs) with a scikit-learn API, plus the concordance index and time-dependent AUC. Students can compare a Cox model with a random survival forest on churn duration data and evaluate them with C-index and the integrated Brier score.
course_use: Advanced Python lab; pip install scikit-survival.

title: survival (R package) v3.8-12
author_source: Terry Therneau, Thomas Lumley et al.; CRAN, released 2026-09-09; LGPL (>=2)
note: Standard R survival toolkit: Surv(), survfit() Kaplan-Meier, coxph(), survreg() parametric models. Students can estimate customer retention curves and hazard drivers, for example time-to-churn by tariff on the Telco or KKBox data, and test proportional hazards with cox.zph().
course_use: Base R churn-duration models; ships with R (recommended package).

title: tidymodels (R meta-package) v1.5.0
author_source: Max Kuhn, Hadley Wickham, Posit; CRAN, released 2026-04-23; MIT
note: Unified R workflow for churn classification: recipes (preprocessing), parsnip (logit, random forest, xgboost), rsample (cross-validation), yardstick (ROC AUC, lift and gain curves) and censored (survival models). Students can build and tune a churn classifier on IBM Telco (7,043 x 21) and compare a logit with a boosted model in one pipeline.
course_use: R predictive churn lab; install.packages('tidymodels').

title: scikit-learn v1.9.1 and XGBoost v3.4.1 (Python)
author_source: scikit-learn developers (BSD-3-Clause, release 2026-09-10); XGBoost contributors / DMLC (Apache-2.0, release 2026-08-15)
note: Standard stack for churn classification: logistic regression, random forests and gradient boosting, plus calibration, ROC/precision-recall, and permutation importance. Students can train churn models on Telco or the bank churn data, build decile lift tables, and translate predicted churn probabilities into expected retained CLV for targeting.
course_use: Python ML churn lab; pip install scikit-learn xgboost.

title: scikit-uplift (sklift) v0.5.1 (Python)
author_source: Maks Shevchenko, Irina Elisova et al.; PyPI release 2022-08-11; MIT
